catalog_quote: Bennett 2016 §6.1: 'Both fixed and mobile stress systems are attested in Mayan languages. Languages with fixed stress fall into two main sub-types: final stress and penultimate stress (Campbell et al. 1986, Kaufman 1990, England 1990, 2001). Final stress (36a) is the norm in K’ichean languages, though it is also found in Mamean (Tectitán Tektitek, Pérez Vail 2007:37-8; some varieties of Southern Mam, England 1990:225-6).' — DiCanio & Bennett §27.3.1: 'Stress is predictable in Mayan languages, with few exceptions. Four distinct patterns of stress assignment are robustly attested within the family: Fixed final stress: K’ichean-branch Mayan languages and Southern Mam (all Eastern Mayan languages of Guatemala).' — Benito Pérez 2016 §2.2 (Palín Poqomam, stress-marked IPA; no rule stated): '[ki.'mikʲ] kimik ‘morir, enfermedad’ ... [ʔis.'kʲ’aχ] isk’aj ‘epazote’ ... [tu.'luɬ] tulul ‘zapote’ ...…

Bennett 2016, PDF p. 27 = printed p. 495, §6.1 STRESS): 'Both fixed and mobile stress systems are attested in Mayan languages. Languages with fixed stress fall into two main sub-types: final stress and penultimate stress (Campbell et al. 1986, Kaufman 1990, England 1990, 2001). Final stress (36a) is the norm in K'ichean languages, though it is also found in Mamean' — exact match; the Kaqchikel exception note (anima, janila) and the phrase-level remark ('stress is phonologically present at the word level even when acoustically weak') are on the same page as the reader says. new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalization: as a K'ichean-branch language, Poqomam is expected to have fixed word-final stress. The only first-hand Poqomam material opened (Benito Pérez 2016, Palín) does not state a rule but marks stress on the final syllable in every one of its 14 polysyllabic IPA transcriptions (e.g. [ki.'mikʲ] 'morir', [ri.si.'w’i:ɬ] 'su humo', [kam’.'laχ] 'doce'), consistent with the generalization.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Poqomam; not marked in Benito Pérez 2016 transcriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Bennett 2016 notes for the K'ichean pattern generally that loanwords and some native words can carry non-final stress (his examples are Kaqchikel: anima, janila); no Poqomam exceptions reported in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Surveys speak of word-level stress; Bennett 2016 adds that in final-stress Mayan languages stress is acoustically stronger phrase-finally but 'phonologically present at the word level even when acoustically weak'. Benito Pérez 2016 forms are citation-form words. Neither survey gives Poqomam data: the statement is second-hand and family-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Poqomam [poc], poqo1253; Glottolog retired the dialect entries Eastern Poqomam (poqo1257, San Luis Jilotepeque) and Southern Poqomam (poqo1255, Palín/Chinautla) into it. The first-hand file opened (Benito Pérez 2016) describes the Palín variety; Smith-Stark 1983 (not opened) describes San Luis Jilotepeque; the 1998 Cholsamaj grammar (not opened) describes Palín. The family-level surveys quoted make no dialect distinction.

sources.note: §2.2 Fonología (pp. 14-19; PDF pp. 29-34) covers consonants, palatalization, coda devoicing, /w'/, /χ/~/h/, vowel length; no sentence about stress anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent acento/acentu/stress/tónic: 0 hits). The IPA transcriptions carry a stress mark and all 14 polysyllabic forms are marked on the final syllable: [ki.'mikʲ] kimik 'morir', [tu.'luɬ] tulul 'zapote', [ʔa.'w’aχ] ab'aj 'piedra', [q’a.'w’is] q'ab'is 'mano', [ri.si.'w’i:ɬ] risib'iil, [kʲa.'ʔam’] ka'ab' 'dos', [kam’.'laχ] kab'laj 'doce', [maɬ.'kaʔn] malka'n, [ʔis.'kʲ’aχ] isk'aj, [ʃa.'ʔaːʍ] xa'aaw…
Phonology section (consonant/vowel tables, allophony) cites Santos Nicolás & Pérez 1998 but says nothing about stress.
